## Part A - Arithmetic Operations
```{r}
a <- 17
b <- 5

a+b
a-b
a*b
a/b

a %% b
a %/% b

2^10
```
## Part B - Basic Data Types
```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i

typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)

class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)

mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```
## Part C - Type Conversion
```{r}
num_string <- "123"
num_val <- as.numeric(num_string)
typeof(num_val)
class(num_val)
mode(num_val)

as.logical(0)
as.logical(1)

bad_string <- "hello123"
as.numeric(bad_string)
```
## Part D - Strings, paste(), and paste0()
```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"

print(first_name)
print(last_name)
cat(first_name, last_name)

full_name <- paste(first_name, last_name)
full_name
paste0(first_name, last_name)

paste(first_name, last_name, sep = "-")

age <- 21
paste0(full_name, "is", age, "years old.")

```
Question #1: Run 17 / 5, 17 %% 5, and 17 %/% 5 side by side. In your own words, explain how these three results relate to each other mathematically.

(Standard division gives you the exact decimal, while integer division drops the extra fraction to leave just a whole number, and modulus tells you what's left over. If you multiply that whole number by the divisor and add the leftover remainder, you get your original number back.)



Question #2: Predict the output of 10 %% 3 and 10 %/% 3 before running the code. Were you correct? If not, explain what you misunderstood.

(10 %% 3 gives 1 because it's the remainder when 10 is divided by 3 and 10 %% 3 gives 3 because that's how many times 3 fits into 10 evenly. My prediction was correct because these operators simply separate division into its whole parts and leftover parts.)

Question #3): x <- 42 and y <- 42L look almost identical, but typeof(x) and typeof(y) give different answers. Explain the difference in your own words.

(Even though both store the number 42, the L suffix forces R to treat it strictly as a whole-number integer, whereas the plain number is stored as a decimal-capable double.)



Question #4: Is typeof() ever different from class() and from mode() for the same object? Look at your results above and explain any case where this happens (or, if you did not see one, explain what you would expect for a matrix or factor).

(Yes, they can differ when higher-level structures (like factors or matrices) store data under the hood as primitive types (typeof) while presenting a specialized class (class).)

Question #5: When you ran the conversion-fail chunk, R produced NA and a warning instead of stopping with an error.

Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?

(R gives a warning instead of crashing so that your script keeps running and you can handle or fix the bad data without losing all your progress.)

What are the risks of this behavior if you don’t read your warnings?

(If you ignore warnings, silent errors or missing data (NA) can sneak into your calculations and ruin your final results without you realizing it.)


Question #6: as.logical(0) and as.logical(1) convert to FALSE and TRUE.

What do you think as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1)` will produce?
( Numbers other than 0 and 1 usually convert to TRUE in R.)



Test it, then explain the rule R seems to be following.
(R treats anything other than zero as TRUE, while strictly zero evaluates to FALSE.)

Question #7: paste() and paste0() produced different results for the same two strings. Explain exactly why, referencing what each function does by default.

(paste() automatically adds a space between items by default, whereas paste0() jams them together with no space at all.)

Question #8: In the strings-numbers chunk, you combined a character string with a numeric variable (age) using paste0() without first converting age to a string.

Did this cause an error? Explain what paste0() does internally to make this work, and how it relates to the type conversions you practiced in Part C.


(It did not cause an error because paste0() automatically converts numbers into text behind the scenes before joining them together, acting similarly to an automatic as.character() conversion.)

Question #9: Some programming languages automatically convert "5" + 5 into 10 without an error. R does not.

Based on what you’ve learned about R’s data types in this lab, why do you think R requires an explicit conversion instead of guessing what the programmer meant?

(R is strict about types to prevent silent bugs, forcing programmers to be explicit rather than guessing wrong and mixing up text with math.)



Question #10:
Suppose a classmate writes a script that reads a column of “numbers” from a text file. The column looks numeric, but when they try sum() on it, R throws an error. Based on everything in this lab (types, typeof()/class()/mode(), conversion, warnings), write a short paragraph explaining what likely went wrong and the steps you’d take to diagnose and fix it.

(The column likely loaded as character text due to a stray symbol or formatting issue, causing sum() to fail. To fix it, check the type using class(), inspect for malformed entries, and explicitly convert the column using as.numeric().)



Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize what you learned about how R handles different data types, and why understanding typeof()/class() and conversion functions matters before doing arithmetic or combining data.

(This lab showed how R handles different data types, from basic numbers and text to logical values, and why it cares so much about how data is stored. Understanding tools like typeof() and conversion functions helps prevent unexpected math errors and stops silent bugs before you try to combine or analyze your data.)
